guidance: Bits only: the page reads the address you paste and never contacts it, the Teredo server or a resolver, so it explains the layout without saying whether the tunnel works or who owns the address. A network-specific NAT64 prefix cannot be recognised from an address at all, so paste yours in the second field; without it, those addresses read as unrecognised. 6to4's relay anycast prefix was deprecated in RFC 7526, so a decodable 6to4 address is not evidence of working connectivity, and an ISATAP identifier only shows which IPv4 address the node claims, not that it is reachable. Every field shown is read straight from the 128 bits; nothing is looked up.
method: The page reads the 128 bits of one address and asks which transition layout produced them, testing 6to4, then Teredo, then NAT64, then ISATAP, because a NAT64 address can end in an interface identifier that would otherwise read as ISATAP's. 6to4 (RFC 3056): the address starts with 2002::/16 and the 32 bits at positions 16 to 47 are the site's public IPv4 address, so the site holds the 2002:V4ADDR::/48 prefix and leaves through the 6to4 relay anycast address 192.88.99.1, whose anycast prefix RFC 7526 deprecated. Teredo (RFC 4380): the address starts with 2001:0::/32, bits 32 to 63 are the Teredo server's IPv4 address, bits 64 to 79 are flags whose only defined bit is 0x8000 (the client's cone-NAT belief), bits 80 to 95 are the client's mapped UDP port and bits 96 to 127 its mapped IPv4 address, both stored with every bit inverted, so the port is that 16-bit field exclusive-ORed with 0xFFFF and the address is that 32-bit field exclusive-ORed with 0xFFFFFFFF; the reserved flag bits must be zero and are reported when they are not. NAT64 (RFC 6052): the address is inside the well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96, or inside a network-specific prefix of 32, 40, 48, 56, 64 or 96 bits that you supply; the IPv4 address follows the prefix, with the first 64 - n bits in positions n to 63, the reserved octet at 64 to 71 skipped, and the remaining bits from position 72, so a /32 keeps all 32 bits at 32 to 63 and a /64 keeps all of them at 72 to 103. That reserved octet must be zero and the bits after the IPv4 address are reserved for future use, so both are reported. ISATAP (RFC 5214): the last 64 bits are the interface identifier 0000:5EFE:w.x.y.z with the four IPv4 octets in network byte order, or 0200:5EFE:w.x.y.z when the u bit marks that IPv4 address as globally unique, and the identifier can sit under a link-local, unique-local or global prefix, which is why ISATAP is matched on the identifier instead of on a prefix. A network-specific NAT64 prefix cannot be recognised from the address alone, so it is a separate field, and when it is supplied and the address falls outside it the page says so instead of guessing. The canonical form shown is RFC 5952. The page refuses rather than guesses: an empty address, spaces or control characters, brackets, a zone ID, a prefix length on the address itself, a second :: marker, groups that are not one to four hexadecimal digits, an embedded IPv4 part that is not four decimal octets, and a prefix field with no length or a length other than the six RFC 6052 allows.
